notes.body:
Zakat (زكاة) comes before all other claims because it was **never truly part of the deceased's wealth** to begin with. Once the threshold (نصاب) is reached and the annual cycle (حول) passes, that portion is held in trust for the poor — not possessed. Settling the estate means returning it before distributing what was actually his.

Hajj (حج) comes next because it is one of the five pillars, a universal duty owed to Allah by every capable Muslim. The one-fifth (خمس) follows because, while deeply binding, it is the **particular claim of the Imam** and the Prophet's family — a more inward channel, but one that comes after the universal. Expiation (كفارة) and al-Shurwa (الشروى) settle last of all, because they are the most private: broken vows, unmended fasts, and the soul's own ransom lie between an individual and Allah alone.

The sequence traces **a movement from the communal to the solitary**:

- Zakat: owed to the community of the poor
- Hajj: owed to Allah as a universal pillar
- Khums: owed to the Imam as the living axis of the faith
- Expiation: owed for personal transgressions against one's covenants
- Al-Shurwa: owed as the soul's own ransom before Allah

Imam al-Muizz li-Din Allah described zakat as **mutual consolation** — all of creation as a single soul, every limb turning toward the limb in pain. That image carries the logic of the whole: the estate first heals the community, then honours the pillars that hold it upright, and only then settles the private account the individual soul owes in its own reckoning with Allah.

etymology: زكاة (purification): from the root ز-ك-و, conveying both purity and growth. To زكّى is to cleanse; but the same root describes a plant shooting upward. Giving زكاة does both — it purifies the remaining wealth while promising its growth in blessing. The word fuses an act of subtraction with a promise of increase.

خمس (one-fifth): from the root خ-م-س, the Arabic word for five. The obligation is named after the fraction itself: one share taken from every five. The same root gives الخميس, Thursday, the fifth day. In every form, the root simply counts — pointing to position, fraction, and portion.

كفارة (expiation): from the root ك-ف-ر, meaning to cover. To كفّر a sin is to neutralise and bury it through atonement. Notably, the same root gives كافر — one who covers over the truth of faith. Expiation and rejection share one root; what differs is whether what is covered is one's own sin or Allah's light.

نصاب (threshold): from the root ن-ص-ب, meaning to set upright, to erect. A نصب is a marker planted in the ground. The نصاب is the minimum amount "erected" as a boundary — the point at which an obligation stands up and becomes binding on the owner.

حول (annual cycle): from the root ح-و-ل, meaning to turn, to revolve, to change state. The حول is the year that has "turned over." The same root gives تحوّل (transformation) and حال (condition, state). Time in Arabic is understood as a turning; the حول is the full arc of that turn.

notes.body:
When our master Zayd ibn Muhammad says that two hundred dirhams "are two covenants," he is **reading the outward in the light of the inward** — a practice at the heart of Ismaili thought. The silver threshold (نصاب) is not just a financial boundary; it is a marker of its owner's full standing in the covenantal life of faith.

The two covenants are the **foundational pair** that together make a believer whole:

- The first is the covenant with the Prophet — a commitment to the outward religious law (شريعة), the visible, shared dimension of the faith.
- The second is the covenant with the Imam — a commitment to the inward spiritual reality (حقيقة), the living knowledge that flows through the line of the Imam in every age.

Neither covenant alone is sufficient; a believer who holds only one is like a body with one eye — alive, but unable to see the full depth of what lies before them.

When the text tells us that whoever owns two hundred dirhams is **forbidden to receive zakat or charity**, it speaks in the same voice: this person has crossed the threshold of need — outwardly in silver, inwardly in covenantal standing — and now bears the full privilege of giving, not taking.

The role of the full year (حول) strengthens this reading. A covenant is not a single moment of declaration; it is a **sustained, living bond**. The turning of the full year over one's wealth symbolizes that endurance — the passing of time proves the covenant is not abandoned but held.

The esoteric interpretation (تأويل) reveals that **the zakat of our silver and the zakat of our soul are never truly separate**: every outward obligation is a mirror in which we see our covenants, our standing before Allah, our place in the body of the faithful.

notes.quote: upon whoever owns two hundred dirhams there are five dirhams, and the two hundred are two covenants
etymology: عهد (covenant): from root ع-ه-د, meaning to bind oneself in a solemn commitment. The root captures a mutual, held obligation — something entrusted between two parties. That is why عهد extends to mean both "covenant" and "era": the covenant defines and governs the very time in which it is honored.

نصاب (threshold): from root ن-ص-ب, meaning to erect, to stand upright, to plant firmly in the ground. Just as a boundary post is driven into the earth to mark where one territory ends and another begins, the نصاب marks the exact point at which an obligation rises.

حول (year): from root ح-و-ل, meaning to turn, to revolve, to shift. The full revolution of twelve months is built into the word itself — to "turn" through time. It is this completion of the circle that triggers the zakat due.

تأويل (esoteric interpretation): from root أ-و-ل, meaning to return to the first, to trace something back to its origin. The word means "the act of taking something back to where it came from" — to interpret is to restore the hidden meaning to its rightful surface.
